item.title: $168M loan guarantee provided for First Nations' investment in LNG pipeline
item.description: A dozen First Nations are being provided a loan guarantee to support their investment in a pipeline feeding natural gas to the LNG Canada plant.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: VANCOUVER — A dozen First Nations in British Columbia are being provided a roughly $168-million loan guarantee to support their investment in a pipeline that feeds natural gas to the LNG Canada plant.  It’s the fifth transaction the federal Canada Indigenous Loan Guarantee Corp. has closed since the agency was set up in 2024, with the goal of helping make it more affordable for First Nations, Métis and Inuit communities to share in the economic benefits of major projects.  The 12 nations that make up the CGL First Nations Limited Partnership are investing in the entity that holds TC Energy’s interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, which delivers gas from northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada plant and tanker port Kitimat, B.C.  “This investment represents a historic milestone for our Nations and a new chapter in our relationship with Coastal GasLink,” said Corrina Leween, director of the First Nations partnership, in a news release Thursday.  “It reflects years of work to advance Indigenous participation in major infrastructure projects and to create a stronger role for our nations in shaping the economic future of our territories.” The investment is the second planned Indigenous investment deal related to Coastal GasLink. In October, another group representing five First Nations announced it had invested $65.3 million of its own funds in TC’s Coastal GasLink subsidiary.  For major projects to happen, the support of affected Indigenous communities is crucial, federal Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said in an interview Thursday.  “As nations become more comfortable with projects, as they become more comfortable with different forms of participation, we’ll see more and more equity ownership,” he said. “It’s the ultimate form of ownership in a project because it means you have real participation and upside from the project.” TC chief executive François Poirier said in a news release that the deal reflects the strength of the relationships the company has developed along the pipeline corridor over more than a decade. “This transaction demonstrates what is possible when Indigenous communities, industry and governments come together with a shared commitment to creating opportunities that deliver benefits over the long term,” he said.  TC has given the green light to a project that would expand the capacity of Coastal GasLink to serve the second phase of LNG Canada. No new pipeline would be built, but the flow of gas would be increased through pumping power and other upgrades.  For the pipeline expansion, the LNG Canada partners — Shell Canada and four Asian firms — are taking the lead on construction, reducing the exposure to cost overrun and schedule risks for TC and its co-owners in the pipeline.  The initial construction of Coastal GasLink encountered numerous challenges, from blockades by opponents in Wet’suwet’en traditional territory in northern B.C. to disruptions from the COVID-19 pandemic. By the time it was complete in late 2023, the cost had ballooned to $14.5 billion from $6.6 billion five years earlier. “Look how far we’ve come. We’ve come from a place where a project like this, there was no shared vision, to a place where the project is performing, it’s generating revenues for the people of British Columbia, for the people of Canada, and now — really importantly — for the First Nations all along its route,” Hodgson said.  Within B.C. First Nations, sentiment toward Coastal GasLink is divided.  A majority of Wet’suwet’en elected band councils supported the pipeline, while some traditional hereditary chiefs resisted it. “We respect every Nation’s right to self-determination, and the reality is this project destroyed our lands without our consent,” Hereditary Chief Na’Moks said in an emailed statement after Thursday’s announcement.  TC and the Indigenous groups hold a collective 35 per cent interest in Coastal GasLink, with KKR Co. and Alberta Investment Management Corp. owning the rest.  “TC Energy is further divesting from CGL, a project for which TC Energy’s estimates for the cost of construction doubled, and now the federal government is encouraging Indigenous finances to back it, tying those to the risk and uncertainty of the pipeline and LNG business,” said Gwii Lok’im Gibuu, a member of the Gitxan First Nation and co-executive director of the Skeena Watershed Conservation Coalition.  --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

item.title: ‘Kraft Dinner’ budget: Mayor’s comments prompt second protest at City Hall
item.description: Protesters gathered in front of City Hall Thursday afternoon to protest comments made by Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.
item.dc:creator: Daniel J. Rowe
item.content:encoded: After starting a swirl of memes, mockery and malcontent over Kraft Dinner comments, protesters gathered in front of City Hall Thursday afternoon to protest Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada. A protest began at 1 p.m. following the nearly 10 per cent tax increase announced earlier this week, followed by Martinez Ferrada’s since walked-back statements. “It’s just like when you’re putting together your personal budget: If you know you’re going to have less money next year, well, you have to make some choices,” she said in a Quartre95 interview. “Let’s be honest, maybe sometimes we’ll eat a little more Kraft Dinner because we can’t afford filet mignon.” The mayor recorded a social media post the following day saying “it was pretty tactless.” “What I meant was that when a city makes choices, it’s the same as when you make personal choices,” she said. “In this instance, the city has to choose between paying for new parks or filling potholes, and I’m going to choose filling potholes.” Protesters came armed with Kraft Dinner, pans, stoves and ingredients, with the apparent intention to make the Canadian household staple a political flashpoint. Raúl Garate organized the protest, saying the tax hike will affect home owners, but also tenants. “I’m not against the fact that we need to take care of our of our city because it is in dire need of love,” he said, adding that he was concerned about the burden on working Montrealers. “You have people, like working-class people, that struggle so much to make their ends meet that will have to also consider this new tax hike.” Montreal’s budget increased the average municipal tax rate to 9.8 per cent in Montreal. It was the largest increase in 50 years. Martinez Ferrada said the increase was necessary to deal with the city’s aging infrastructure, including water mains, housing and homelessness. Thursday’s protest will be the second this week, as hundreds of demonstrators gathered on Tuesday. Peter Sergakis, owner of hundreds of residential units, bars and restaurants, organized that protest.

item.title: Tech leaders urge to build more data centres in Canada
item.description: Canadian tech leaders gathered by policy group Build Canada have signed an open letter urging the country to build more data centres.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Canadian tech leaders have signed an open letter urging Canada to build more data centres or risk having to rent computing capacity elsewhere. The 35 signatories gathered by policy group Build Canada warn that relying on other countries for data centres will hamper the country’s access and put it at risk of supply disruptions. “The demand for increased compute capacity is here and data centres will be built whether Canada hosts them or not,” the open letter says.  “The only choice in front of us is whether we build it, shape it and earn from it, or rent it from the countries that do. The world will not wait on our decision.” The letter signed by Shopify Inc. president Harley Finkelstein, Neo Financial co-founder Jeff Adamson and Koho chief executive Daniel Eberhard positions data centres as crucial to the adoption of artificial intelligence. It also frames the hulking facilities, which house technology infrastructure, as necessary for internet usage, cancer screening, wildfire prediction and software used to run businesses and governments. In pushing for more data centres, the signatories point to documents received by the federal AI minister in January that suggest Canada had about 337 megawatts of AI data centre capacity.  The signatories point out the government’s own AI strategy estimates Canada will need 5.5 gigawatts of domestic capacity by 2030. “That is 16 times what we have right now,” the letter points out. “We must build data centres, and we must build them faster. Not building them is not an option.” The letter comes as several data centre projects, including some with links to tech giants like Meta and Anthropic, are slated in Canada but face fierce opposition from local communities and environmentalists. Opponents say data centres are noisy and hog water, land and electricity while contributing few jobs relative to their massive footprint. Build Canada’s letter argues data centres use less water than a golf course, are about as loud as refrigerator and only drive up power bills when data centres are connected to small, tight grids, so the facilities should bring their own power.  --- Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

item.title: Global stocks rise and tech shares rebound as U.S. closes for Thanksgiving
item.description: U.S. stock futures also climbed, with the S&P 500 futures up 0.5 per cent. U.S. markets will reopen Friday for a holiday-shortened session.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: HONG KONG — Shares advanced in Europe and Asia on Thursday while U.S. markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday. Buying of stocks tied to artificial intelligence helped push benchmarks in Asia higher, though some profit-taking by investors toward the end of the day pared those gains. Investors have been growing cautious about the AI trade. They also are watching for impacts from the latest tariff hikes Washington plans to impose on China, Japan, the European Union and other trading partners. In early European trading, Germany’s DAX jumped 1.9 per cent to 25,180.12, while France’s CAC 40 climbed 1.8 per cent to 8,126.47. Britain’s FTSE 100 added 1.6 per cent to 10,591.83. U.S. stock futures also climbed, with the S&P 500 futures up 0.5 per cent. U.S. markets will reopen Friday for a holiday-shortened session. In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rebounded and closed 0.9 per cent higher at 57,499.16. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group jumped 7.3 per cent, while memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings surged 12.6 per cent. Shares of chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron were up 0.6 per cent. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index added 0.3 per cent to 4,711.21 after a 6.2 per cent drop a day earlier. Samsung Electronics gained 0.4 per cent, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix rose 2.2 per cent. Taiwan’s Taiex was 2.5 per cent higher. But shares of its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., edged 0.2 per cent lower. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index was 1.2 per cent higher at 22,226.88. The Shanghai Composite index was up less than 0.1 per cent at 3,476.88. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.8 per cent to 8,763.80. India’s Sensex rose 0.5 per cent. Wall Street closed mixed ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The benchmark S&P 500 index lost 0.3 per cent Wednesday after falling as much as 3.2 per cent earlier in the day. The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed 0.6 per cent lower, after recovering from a drop of as much as 4.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average picked up 0.3 per cent. Nvidia fell 3.9 per cent as AI shares lost steam for a second day after Jensen Huang’s comeback as CEO. On Wednesday, S&P Global Ratings warned it could downgrade Nvidia’s credit rating over concerns surrounding its management and governance. Broadcom, which had fallen sharply earlier in the day, was 0.1 per cent lower at the close. Anthropic, which began public trading last week, recovered from an early drop and ended 1.1 per cent higher, though still below its IPO, or initial public offering, price of US$83 per share. In commodities trading, oil prices climbed early Thursday as tensions in the Middle East persisted even as global oil supply continued to recover. Brent crude, the international standard, was 0.5 per cent higher at $91.09 per barrel. It was trading at approximately $72 a barrel before the war began in late February. Benchmark U.S. crude gained one per cent to $84.51 per barrel. Recent reports of vessels being targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global oil transport, have contributed to concerns over oil flows and “brought supply risks back into focus,” ING commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in a commentary Thursday. The U.S. dollar rose to 159.30 Japanese yen from 159.16 yen. The euro was trading at $1.0968, down from $1.0974. Chan Ho-him, The Associated Press
